name: Authentication
summary: Proving who a user is, before anyone decides what they may do.
howItWorks: Authentication answers “who are you?”; authorization (see IAM) then answers “what may you do?”. A user proves identity with something they know (a password), something they have (a phone or security key) or something they are (a fingerprint), and multi-factor authentication (MFA) asks for two of them. A password is never stored as typed: the server keeps a salted, deliberately slow hash such as Argon2id or bcrypt, so a stolen database can’t simply be read back. After a successful login the app has to remember the user on every later request. It can hand the browser a random session ID in a cookie and keep the session on the server, which is easy to revoke, or it can issue a signed token such as a JSON Web Token (JWT) that any service can check without a lookup, which is hard to revoke before it expires. Most apps no longer check passwords themselves: they redirect the user to an identity provider (Google, Microsoft Entra ID or a customer’s own directory) using OpenID Connect or SAML, and get back a signed statement of who the user is. Passkeys go further and replace the password with a key pair: the private key never leaves the user’s device and only signs challenges for the site it was created for, which makes it resistant to phishing.
analogy: Checking in at a hotel. The front desk checks your passport once (authentication) and gives you a key card (the session). The card opens your room and the gym but not the kitchen (authorization), and it stops working when you check out.
useWhen: Any app where users have their own data, settings or permissions
Selling to companies whose IT team wants staff to sign in through their own directory (SAML or OIDC single sign-on) and be removed automatically when they leave (SCIM)
Protecting admin and high-value accounts with MFA or passkeys
avoidWhen: Writing your own password storage, reset emails and MFA when a maintained library or provider does it; the details are easy to get wrong
Treating a valid login as permission: being signed in says who someone is, not what they may touch
Long-lived JWTs as sessions when you need instant logout or account suspension, unless you add a deny list
example: A project-management SaaS lets individuals sign up with email and a passkey, or with a password plus a code from an authenticator app. When a 2,000-person company buys it, their IT team connects the app to the company directory: employees click “Sign in with SSO”, the app redirects them to the company’s identity provider over SAML or OIDC, and the app never sees their passwords. SCIM pushes joiners and leavers, so an employee who leaves on Friday loses access when the directory disables them, not when someone remembers to delete the account.

source: # 1. The app redirects the browser to the identity provider (OIDC authorization code flow with PKCE)
# 2. After the user signs in, the provider sends the browser back with a one-time code
# 3. The app's server swaps the code for tokens, proving it started the flow
# 4. The id_token is a signed JWT saying who the user is; the app checks it and starts a session

diagram.caption: Most requests carry a valid session cookie and go straight to the app. Requests without one are redirected to the identity provider; after the user signs in, the browser comes back with a code, the app swaps it for tokens and starts a session. The slow round trips are logins.

sections.title: The standards you’ll meet
sections.intro: They solve different problems and are often used together: a B2B app might take OIDC logins from individuals, SAML from enterprise customers, SCIM for provisioning and WebAuthn for passkeys.

rows.label: OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749, 2012)
values: Lets an app get limited access to an API on a user’s behalf. Authorization, not login.
“Allow this app to read your calendar”

rows.label: OpenID Connect (2014)
values: An identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0: adds an ID token saying who signed in
JSON; ID token is a JWT
“Sign in with Google”, modern enterprise SSO

rows.label: SAML 2.0 (2005)
values: Single sign-on: the identity provider sends a signed assertion about the user
Enterprise SSO from a company directory

rows.label: SCIM 2.0 (RFC 7643/7644, 2015)
values: Creates, updates and deactivates accounts from a directory

rows.label: WebAuthn / FIDO2 (2019)
values: Sign-in with a key pair held by the device, scoped to one site

notes: A JWT (RFC 7519) is just a signed, compact token format; OIDC uses it, but so do many home-grown session schemes.

story: Passwords came with time-sharing. Robert Morris and Ken Thompson’s 1979 account of Unix password security recalls that the first Unix kept everyone’s actual passwords in a file that had to be guarded, and that on MIT’s CTSS an editing mix-up once printed the password file on every terminal at login. Unix moved to storing only an encrypted form, made it deliberately slow, and added a 12-bit random salt so that identical passwords looked different and precomputed attacks stopped working. bcrypt (Provos and Mazières, 1999) made the slowness adjustable as hardware got faster, and Argon2, winner of the 2013 to 2015 Password Hashing Competition, also made attackers pay in memory.

As people collected accounts on dozens of sites, the work moved to identity providers. SAML 2.0 (2005) let a company’s directory vouch for its staff at other organisations’ apps. OAuth 2.0 (2012) standardised how an app gets limited access to an API on a user’s behalf; it is an authorization protocol and says nothing about who the user is. OpenID Connect, ratified in February 2014, added a proper identity layer on top: an ID token, a signed JWT that says who signed in, to whom, and when.

Passwords and one-time codes can be typed into a fake site, so the industry moved to public-key credentials. The W3C published Web Authentication (WebAuthn) as a Recommendation in March 2019, and in May 2022 Apple, Google and Microsoft committed to passkeys that sync across a user’s devices. NIST’s 2025 guidelines now tell US federal systems to offer a phishing-resistant option, and to stop forcing periodic password changes and composition rules.

choices.choice: Store a salted, slow hash, never the password
choices.why: A password file will eventually leak. Morris and Thompson salted and slowed down Unix’s hashes so a stolen file would be expensive to crack; bcrypt and Argon2 let that cost grow with hardware.

choices.choice: Delegate login to an identity provider
choices.why: With redirects (SAML, OIDC) the app never sees the user’s password, users keep one login, and an employer can switch off access centrally when someone leaves.

choices.choice: Build identity on OAuth 2.0 instead of a new protocol
choices.why: Sites already used OAuth to call each other’s APIs. OpenID Connect reused that machinery for login, adding only a signed ID token, so libraries and providers could support both.

choices.choice: Key pairs bound to a site, not shared secrets
choices.why: A password or SMS code can be typed into a fake site. A WebAuthn credential is scoped to the site that created it and only signs a challenge, so there is nothing reusable to steal.

timeline.text: Morris and Thompson describe salted, slow password hashing in Unix
Provos and Mazières present bcrypt, with an adjustable cost
OpenID Connect ratified by the OpenID Foundation
Argon2 wins the Password Hashing Competition; JWT and SCIM 2.0 published as RFCs
Apple, Google and Microsoft commit to passkeys
